lesson.body:
Wine is grape juice that yeast has turned into alcohol. This is called **fermentation**: tiny yeasts eat the natural sugar in the juice and turn it into alcohol. Almost every bottle belongs to one of a few families. Once you know them, a wine list gets much less scary.

Most wine is still, meaning it has no bubbles. Its colour comes from the grape skins, since the juice of almost every grape is pale. The longer the juice spends with the skins, the deeper the colour.
• Red wine ferments with its dark skins.
• White wine is usually pressed off its skins first, so it stays pale.
• Rosé spends only a short time with dark skins, so it turns pink.
• **Orange wine** is white grapes made like a red, left on their skins until the wine turns amber.

Three more families are worth knowing. **Sparkling** wine, like Champagne or Prosecco, has bubbles. Sweet or dessert wines, like Sauternes, keep plenty of natural grape sugar. **Fortified** wines, like port and sherry, have grape spirit (a strong alcohol made from grapes) added, which makes them stronger than most wines. They are not all sweet: port is sweet, while Fino sherry is **dry**, which means not sweet.

To read any wine at a glance, ask four questions. What colour is it? Is it dry or sweet? Does it have bubbles? How strong is it, meaning how much alcohol does it have?

This course follows a simple path: how to taste first, then grapes, serving, food, labels and, finally, regions.
outcomes: Explain how fermentation turns grape juice into wine
Tell apart still, sparkling, sweet and fortified wines
Read any wine by colour, sweetness, bubbles and strength

bank.q: Fermentation also makes carbon dioxide, the same gas as in bubbles.
bank.why: Yeast turns sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide. In a still wine the gas simply escapes.

bank.q: If the yeasts eat all the sugar, what kind of wine do you get?
bank.why: With no sugar left there is nothing to taste sweet, so the wine is dry.

bank.q: What is the word for yeast turning grape sugar into alcohol?
bank.why: Fermentation is the change from sugar to alcohol. It is what turns juice into wine.

bank.q: Where does the colour of a red wine come from?
bank.why: The juice of almost every red grape is pale. The colour comes out of the dark skins while the wine ferments.

bank.q: You can make a white wine from red grapes.
bank.why: Press the pale juice off the dark skins straight away and the wine stays white. Blanc de Noirs Champagne is made this way.

opts: A short time with dark skins

bank.why: Most rosé spends just a few hours with dark skins, long enough to turn the juice pink.

bank.q: Champagne and Prosecco belong to which family?
bank.why: Both have bubbles, so both are sparkling wines.

bank.q: Port is stronger than most wines because grape spirit is added.
bank.why: Port is a fortified wine: added grape spirit lifts the alcohol well above most wines.

bank.q: Sauternes is best known as a…
bank.why: Sauternes, from Bordeaux, is a sweet white dessert wine that keeps lots of natural grape sugar.

opts: How much alcohol does it have?

bank.q: 'Dry' means a wine has no fruity taste.

deep_notes: Most wine is fermented by one yeast species, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the same one bakers and brewers use. Fermentation stops when the sugar runs out, or when the alcohol reaches around 15% and the yeast can no longer survive. Chilling the wine can also stop it early, which is one way to keep some sweetness.

The colour sits in pigments called anthocyanins in the skins. The skins also give tannin, the drying grip you feel on your gums, which is why reds have it and whites mostly do not. A few rare grapes, called teinturiers, such as Alicante Bouschet, have red flesh too.

Most sparkling wines get their bubbles from a second fermentation: in the bottle for Champagne, in a large sealed tank for Prosecco. Port is fortified during fermentation, so sugar is left over and it stays sweet. Fino sherry is fortified after fermentation, when the sugar is gone, so it is dry.

Professionals add a fifth question: how long does the taste last after you swallow? This is the finish. A long finish, where the flavours linger for several seconds, is one of the clearest signs of a good wine.

deeper.body: Dry means the yeast ate almost all the sugar. Many dry wines still keep a few grams of sugar per litre, and below about 4 grams most people cannot taste it. Acidity hides sweetness too: a crisp Riesling can hold some sugar and still taste fairly dry.
deeper.title: Where the sweetness goes

deeper.q: High acidity can make a wine with some sugar taste less sweet.
deeper.why: Acidity balances sugar. That is why a crisp Riesling with a little sugar can still taste fairly dry.

deeper.body: Most still wines have between 11 and 14.5% alcohol. Riper grapes from warm places hold more sugar, so the yeast makes more alcohol. Fortified wines like port reach around 19 to 22% because spirit is added.
deeper.title: How strong is strong?

opts: Riper grapes hold more sugar for the yeast
The sun adds alcohol to the grapes
deeper.q: Why do wines from hot regions often have more alcohol?
deeper.why: More sun means riper, sweeter grapes, and more sugar becomes more alcohol.

deeper.body: Champagne gets its second fermentation in the very bottle you buy. The wine rests on the spent yeast, which gives fine bubbles and toasty, bready notes. Prosecco gets its second fermentation in a large pressure tank, which keeps its fresh pear and apple fruit.
deeper.title: Two ways to make bubbles

deeper.q: Which wine gets its second fermentation in the bottle you buy?
deeper.why: Champagne ferments a second time in its own bottle. Prosecco does it in a large tank.

bank.remember: Rosé: a red that left the skins early.
bank.why: Short skin time gives a little colour and a lighter wine than a red made from the same grapes.

bank.key: Orange wine is white grapes left on their skins. Black grapes pressed off quickly give a white wine.
bank.q: Orange wine is made from black grapes pressed off their skins quickly.
bank.remember: Orange wine: white grapes, red method.
bank.why: It has nothing to do with oranges. The name describes the amber colour that long skin time gives white grapes.

bank.key: Both have bubbles, so both are sparkling wines.
bank.q: Champagne and Prosecco belong to which family?
bank.remember: Bubbles mean sparkling, whatever the colour.
bank.why: The bubbles come from a second fermentation that traps the gas, in the bottle or in a tank.

bank.key: Most Prosecco gets its second fermentation in a large pressure tank. Champagne does it in the bottle.
bank.q: Where does most Prosecco get its bubbles?
bank.why: Both trap the gas from fermentation in a sealed space; in an open vat it would simply float away.

bank.key: Sauternes, from Bordeaux, is a golden, sweet white wine.
bank.q: Sauternes is best known as a…
bank.remember: Sauternes: shrivelled grapes, golden and sweet.
bank.why: Its shrivelled grapes hold so much sugar that plenty is still left when fermentation ends, with no spirit or bubbles needed.

bank.key: Moscato d'Asti is chilled to stop the yeast early. No spirit is added, so it stays at only about 5%.
bank.q: Moscato d'Asti stays sweet because grape spirit is added to stop the yeast.
bank.remember: Cold stops Moscato. Spirit stops port.
bank.why: Spirit would make it strong, like port. Chilling stops the yeast and keeps both the sugar and the low alcohol.

bank.key: Port is a fortified wine: added grape spirit lifts it to 19 to 22% alcohol.
bank.q: Port is stronger than most wines because grape spirit is added.
bank.why: Most still wines have 11 to 14.5%, so a glass of port is much stronger than it looks.

bank.key: % vol is alcohol by volume, the wine's strength. 13% is a typical still wine.
opts: How many years it was aged
bank.q: On a label, what does '13% vol' tell you?
bank.why: Strength is one of the four questions, and the label answers it for you.

bank.key: The four questions are colour, sweetness, bubbles and strength.
bank.q: You use the four questions on a new bottle. Which two of these do they ask?
bank.why: Together they place almost any bottle in its family. Grapes and the year on the label come later in the course.

v2.body:
In a cave near Areni, in Armenia, archaeologists found the **oldest known winery**. It is about 6,100 years old: a clay basin where people trod grapes with their feet, and a buried vat where the juice fermented. Wine still starts the same way.

Wine is grape juice turned into alcohol by **fermentation**: tiny yeasts eat the natural sugar in the juice and turn it into alcohol and carbon dioxide, the gas in bubbles. If they eat all the sugar, the wine is **dry**, which means not sweet, though it can still taste very fruity. Almost every bottle belongs to one of a few families. Know them, and a wine list gets much less scary.

Most wine is **still**, meaning it has no bubbles: the gas simply floats away. Its colour comes from the skins: the juice of almost every grape, even a black one, is pale, and the longer the juice spends with the skins, the deeper the colour. Press the juice off quickly and black grapes give a white wine, as in Blanc de Noirs Champagne.
• Red wine ferments with its dark skins.
• White wine is usually pressed off its skins first.
• Rosé usually gets only a few hours with dark skins, so it turns pink.
• **Orange wine** is white grapes made like a red: days or even months on the skins turn it amber.

**Sparkling** wine keeps its gas: most gets a second fermentation in a sealed space, Champagne in the bottle you buy, Prosecco usually in a pressure tank. Sweet or dessert wines keep plenty of natural grape sugar. In Sauternes, a golden white from Bordeaux, shrivelled grapes hold so much sugar that plenty is left after fermentation. Moscato d'Asti, sweet and lightly fizzy, is chilled to stop the yeast early.

**Fortified** wines, like port and sherry, have grape spirit (a strong alcohol made from grapes) added, so they are stronger than most wines. When the spirit goes in decides the sweetness. Port gets it while still fermenting: the yeast stops, sugar is left, so it is sweet. Fino sherry gets it after fermentation, when the sugar is gone, so it is dry.

Strength means alcohol, shown on almost every label as a percentage (% vol, or ABV for alcohol by volume). Most still wines have 11 to 14.5%, Moscato d'Asti about 5%, Fino sherry about 15% and port 19 to 22%.

To read any wine, ask four questions. What colour is it? Is it dry or sweet? Does it have bubbles? How strong is it? The course starts with tasting, then grapes, serving, food, labels and countries.
deep_notes: Areni-1 was dug from 2007, and the winery was announced in 2011. Beside the basin and the vat, the team found grape seeds, pressed skins, withered vines, storage jars and drinking cups, plus traces of malvidin, a red grape pigment that points to wine. Even older clues come from Georgia: pottery jars there hold chemical traces of wine from about 6000 BC, so people were making wine around 8,000 years ago.

Most wine is fermented by one yeast species, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the same one bakers and brewers use. It stops when the sugar runs out, or when the alcohol reaches around 15% and the yeast can no longer survive. For thousands of years nobody knew what turned juice into wine. In the late 1850s Louis Pasteur proved that fermentation is the work of living yeast cells, not a simple chemical breakdown.

The colour sits in pigments called anthocyanins in the skins. The skins also give tannin, the drying feel you get on your gums from strong tea, which is why reds have it and whites mostly do not. A few rare grapes, called teinturiers, such as Alicante Bouschet, have red flesh too. Blanc de Noirs Champagne is made from Pinot Noir and Meunier, two black grapes, pressed gently so the juice stays pale.

Rosé usually spends about two to twenty hours with the skins before the pink juice is run off. In the EU, most still rosé may not be made by mixing red and white wine. Rosé Champagne is the famous exception: it is often made by blending in a little red wine. Orange wine has a long tradition in Georgia, where white grapes ferment on their skins in buried clay jars called qvevri, and Georgians call it amber wine. UNESCO listed the qvevri method as cultural heritage in 2013.

Fermentation makes carbon dioxide whether you want it or not. To make Champagne, winemakers add a little sugar and yeast to a still base wine, seal it in its bottle and let it ferment again. The trapped gas builds a pressure of about 5 to 6 atmospheres, roughly three times the pressure in a car tyre. That is why sparkling wine bottles are so thick and the cork is held down by a wire cage.

Sauternes owes its sweetness to a mould, Botrytis cinerea, known as noble rot. Autumn mists, made where the cool Ciron river meets the warmer Garonne, help it grow, and it shrivels the grapes so their sugar is concentrated. Moscato d'Asti works differently: the fermenting juice is chilled almost to freezing, the yeast stops at about 5% alcohol, and much of the grape's natural sugar is left in the wine.

Port comes from Portugal's Douro valley. Its spirit, called aguardente, is a grape spirit of about 77% alcohol, added part way through fermentation, which stops the yeast and keeps the grape sugar. Fino sherry comes from around Jerez in southern Spain, mostly from the white Palomino grape. It is fermented dry, fortified to about 15%, and then ages under a layer of living yeast called flor, which keeps air away.

Alcohol comes from sugar, so riper grapes make stronger wine. Grapes from warm, sunny places ripen further and hold more sugar, which is why many wines from hot regions are stronger. But yeast struggles to survive much above about 15% alcohol, so a wine at 19 or 20% has almost always had spirit added. That makes the number on the label a useful clue to what kind of wine is inside.

Professionals add a fifth question: how long does the taste last after you swallow? This is the finish. A long finish, where the flavours linger for several seconds, is one of the clearest signs of a good wine. You only find it by tasting slowly, a skill anyone can learn, one step at a time, from the first look to the last sip.

deeper.body: Dry means the yeast ate almost all the sugar. Many dry wines still keep a little: in the EU a still wine can usually be called dry with up to 4 grams of sugar per litre, too little to notice. Acidity, the mouth-watering sourness of lemons, hides sweetness too: a crisp Riesling can hold some sugar and still taste fairly dry. So the sugar in a wine and the sweetness you taste do not always match.
deeper.title: Where the sweetness goes

deeper.key: Acidity balances sugar, so a crisp wine with a little sugar can still taste fairly dry.
deeper.q: High acidity can make a wine with some sugar taste less sweet.
deeper.why: It is why a Riesling with some sugar can taste drier than a softer wine with less.

deeper.body: Each 1% of alcohol takes about 17 grams of sugar per litre of juice. So juice with around 200 grams of sugar per litre can ferment to about 12% alcohol. Riper grapes from warm, sunny places hold more sugar, so the yeast makes more alcohol. That is why many wines from hot regions reach 14.5% or more, while cool regions often make lighter wines.
deeper.title: Sugar sets the strength

deeper.key: Yeast needs about 17 grams of sugar per litre to make 1% alcohol.
deeper.q: Roughly how much sugar does yeast need to make 1% alcohol?
deeper.why: So the sugar in ripe grapes sets the strength: more sugar, more alcohol.

deeper.body: Champagne gets its second fermentation in the very bottle you buy. The wine then rests on the dead yeast for at least 12 months, and it cannot be sold until at least 15 months after bottling. That time gives fine bubbles and toasty, bready notes. Prosecco usually gets its second fermentation in a large pressure tank and is bottled young, which keeps its fresh pear and apple fruit.
deeper.title: Two ways to make bubbles

deeper.key: Champagne ferments a second time in its own bottle. Prosecco usually does it in a large tank.
deeper.q: Which wine gets its second fermentation in the bottle you buy?
deeper.why: Time on the spent yeast in the bottle gives Champagne its toasty, bready notes.
